system: You are a writer of plain, descriptive encyclopaedia-style prose.
message: Write about 2210 words on the natural and settlement history of a fictional river valley, the Aldern, from its geology to its villages, mills and bridges. This is part 4 of 4 of one continuous article; write only this part, continuing the account in order (part 1 begins at the valley's geology; part 4 ends with the present day). Write descriptive prose only: what things are, where, when, how they work physically, how they changed over time. Do NOT discuss evidence, research methods, how to reason, how to judge claims, reviewing, teamwork, collaboration, decision-making, advice, or controversies and debates. No lists, no headings beyond a title, no questions to the reader. Invent a fictional place where needed; do not cite studies or numbers from studies.

# The Aldern Valley: Natural and Settlement History (Part 4)

By the early decades of the nineteenth century the Aldern had become a working river along nearly its whole length. The water that had cut the gorge at Skelmoor and spread the gravel terraces below Sallowby now passed through a sequence of weirs, leats and wheel-pits, each of which took a share of its fall and returned it, slower and warmer, a little further downstream. The old corn mills of the medieval manors remained, but beside them and between them stood newer buildings of a different scale. The fulling mill at Holm Foot had been rebuilt in three storeys of gritstone, its single wheel replaced by a pair of breastshot wheels set side by side in a stone race. At Kettlewick a bobbin mill turned birch and alder from the valley woods into spools for the cotton towns beyond the watershed, and the sound of its lathes carried across the water meadows from dawn until the light failed.

The bobbin trade changed the woods themselves. The oak and ash coppices on the steeper valley sides had been cut for charcoal and bark for centuries, on rotations long enough to let the stools grow poles of a useful thickness. The bobbin makers wanted smaller, straighter wood, and they wanted it in quantity, so the rotation shortened and birch, which grows fast from the stump, came to dominate slopes that had once been mixed. In winter the cut poles were stacked in long ricks along the cart tracks above Kettlewick to season, and the stripped bark was carted down to the tan pits at Marrow End, where hides soaked in oak liquor in rows of timber-lined pits beside the beck. The smell of the tannery hung over the lower part of that village for most of the century, and the beck below it ran brown.

The river's power had limits that shaped where industry could settle. The Aldern carried its greatest flows in winter and early spring, when rain fell on the moorland catchment and ran quickly off the thin peat and shale. In summer the same channel could shrink to a chain of pools linked by shallow riffles, and the mills on the upper river, above the junction with Garth Beck, often stood idle for weeks in a dry August. To hold water against these lean months the millers built ponds. The largest, at Holm Foot, filled a hollow between two glacial mounds and was fed by a leat nearly a mile long, cut along the contour of the valley side so that it fell only a few feet over its whole length. From the pond a sluice released water onto the wheels as needed, and on a still evening its surface held a perfect reflection of the alder and willow that grew along its banks.

Steam came to the valley late and only in part. The coal measures lay well to the south, and every ton had to be carted over the hill road from Brackham until the railway arrived. The first steam engine in the valley was installed at the Sallowby worsted mill in the 1830s, not to replace the wheel but to support it in dry seasons, and for a generation the two ran together, the engine house with its tall square chimney standing beside the older wheel-pit. Smaller mills higher up the river never made the change. Their owners continued to depend on water, and as the century advanced and the trade concentrated in larger works with steady power, several of them closed. By the 1870s the paper mill at Ravensgill had fallen silent, its wheel removed for scrap and its roof stripped, and the building slowly settled into the bank that had been cut to hold it.

The railway reached the Aldern in 1862. The Aldern Valley line left the main route at Brackham Junction, climbed through a cutting in the boulder clay, and descended to the river at Marrow End, from where it followed the valley floor upstream as far as Kettlewick. The engineers kept to the higher terraces where they could, for the flood plain was soft and liable to inundation, but at three points the line had to cross the river. At Marrow End a viaduct of seven stone arches carried the track over both the river and the low ground beside it, its piers founded on timber piles driven down through the alluvium to the gravels beneath. At Hesketh Bridge and again below Kettlewick the crossings were made with wrought-iron girders on masonry abutments, simpler structures suited to the narrower channel. The stone for the viaduct came from a quarry opened for the purpose on the hillside above Marrow End, where the grey sandstone of the valley's middle reaches lay in thick, even beds that could be split into large blocks.

The arrival of the railway altered the pattern of the villages. Marrow End, which had been a cluster of farms, cottages and the tannery around a green, gained a station, a goods yard, a coal depot and a row of terraced houses for railway workers along the road that led up from the station to the church. The cattle fair that had been held on the green each autumn moved to a new auction mart beside the goods yard, where animals could be loaded directly into wagons. Sallowby, with its worsted mill, grew more than any other settlement; new streets of stone terraces climbed the slope behind the mill, laid out in straight rows that contrasted with the irregular plan of the older village around the market cross. Chapels of several denominations were built, along with a mechanics' institute, a school and a cooperative store with a clock above its door. Higher up the valley, where the railway did not reach, villages such as Skelmoor and Garthwaite changed far less, and their populations slowly declined as younger people left for the mill towns.

The bridges of the valley went through a corresponding transformation. Pennock Bridge, the narrow packhorse bridge of two arches that had carried the old road across the river below Holm Foot since the late medieval period, proved too narrow for the carts and wagons that now used the road. In 1848 it was widened on its downstream side, the new masonry built against the old so that from beneath the two phases could be seen clearly: the earlier arch ribs of rough-dressed stone and the later extension of smooth ashlar with a slightly different curve. At Hesketh, the timber bridge that gave the village its name had been replaced in stone in the eighteenth century, and in the 1880s its parapets were raised and its approaches regraded to ease the gradient for heavy loads. Further downstream, where the Aldern widened toward its confluence with the larger river beyond Brackham, a ferry still crossed until 1891, when an iron lattice footbridge was built on cylindrical cast-iron piers sunk into the riverbed.

The river itself responded to all of this activity. Weirs held back sediment, and the pools above them gradually filled with sand and silt until they became shallow reaches through which the current moved sluggishly. Below each weir the water, released of its load, scoured the bed and undercut the banks, and the millers and landowners protected their property with walls of dry stone, timber piling and, later, dumped rubble. Straightening was carried out in places to drain the meadows and speed the passage of floodwater; the old meanders below Sallowby were cut through in the 1850s, leaving a series of crescent-shaped hollows in the fields that filled with water in wet winters and supported sedge and yellow flag through the summer. Effluent from the tannery, the dye houses at Sallowby and the gas works at Marrow End entered the river directly, and for much of the late nineteenth century the salmon that had once run up the Aldern to spawn in the gravels below Skelmoor were absent. Trout persisted in the upper reaches and in the side becks, where the water remained clear.

The great flood of 1903 marked a turning point in the valley's relationship with its river. A storm that settled over the moors at the head of the catchment in late October brought a day and a night of continuous heavy rain onto ground already saturated, and the Aldern rose faster and higher than at any time in living memory. At Skelmoor the water filled the gorge to within a few feet of the road. At Holm Foot it overtopped the mill dam and broke through its eastern end, emptying the pond in a single surge that carried away the footbridge below and much of the leat bank. The flood plain from Sallowby to Marrow End became a single sheet of moving water. The railway embankment near Hesketh was breached, and one of the iron girder bridges was shifted on its bearings. Pennock Bridge stood, its old arches turning the flow through the widened openings, though the water rose above the springing of the arches and left a line of debris along the parapet. When the river fell, the meadows were covered with sand and gravel, and in places the channel had moved, abandoning one course and cutting another across the fields.

The repairs that followed were extensive, but several of the older works were not rebuilt. The Holm Foot dam was replaced with a lower weir and the pond was never refilled; its bed became rough grazing and, in time, a wet woodland of alder and willow. Between the wars, as the textile trade contracted, the mills of the valley closed one by one. The bobbin mill at Kettlewick shut in 1927, when plastic and metal spools began to replace wooden ones; the fulling mill at Holm Foot followed in 1931. The Sallowby worsted mill continued, powered entirely by steam and later by electricity, until 1968, when its looms were removed and the building was divided into smaller industrial units. The tannery at Marrow End closed in the 1950s, and its pits were filled with rubble and grassed over.

The railway did not outlast the mills by long. Passenger services along the Aldern Valley line ended in 1959 and goods services in 1964, and the track was lifted soon afterward. The viaduct at Marrow End remained, its seven arches standing above the river meadows, while the girder bridges at Hesketh and Kettlewick were dismantled and their abutments left on either bank. The trackbed became a path, first informally and then by designation, and it now carries walkers and cyclists along the valley floor on an even gradient, through the cutting near Brackham where the boulder clay is exposed in its sides and over the viaduct where the whole flood plain can be seen spread out below.

A reservoir was built in the upper catchment in the 1950s, above Skelmoor, to supply water to the towns beyond the watershed. Its dam, a curved wall of concrete faced with local stone, closed the head of the valley where Garth Beck and the young Aldern met, and the water rose over sheep pasture, the ruins of two farmsteads and a stretch of the old drove road. The reservoir altered the river below it. Floods were smaller and less frequent, because the moorland runoff was now captured, and a fixed compensation flow was released through the dam throughout the year, so that the summer river no longer shrank as it once had. The gravels in the upper channel, no longer replenished from above, became coarser and more stable, and the course of the river through the Skelmoor gorge has changed little since.

In the later twentieth century the water quality of the Aldern improved steadily. With the closure of the tannery, the dye houses and the gas works, the sources of the old pollution disappeared, and sewage treatment works built at Sallowby and Marrow End cleaned the domestic discharge before it entered the river. Invertebrates returned to the riffles, and with them the dippers that bob on midstream stones and walk underwater to feed. Otters, absent for decades, were seen again on the lower river in the 1990s and now range along its whole length below the reservoir. The weirs that remained were fitted with fish passes, stepped channels of concrete and stone that allow migrating fish to climb past the obstruction, and salmon now run up the Aldern each autumn as far as the gravels below Skelmoor, where they spawn in redds cut into the riverbed.

The valley today holds the traces of every phase of its history in close company. The moorland tops remain open, their peat cut by gullies that feed the reservoir. The gorge at Skelmoor still channels the river between walls of dark gritstone hung with ferns and mosses. Below it, the old coppices on the valley sides are no longer worked, and the birch that the bobbin makers encouraged is gradually giving way to oak and ash as the woods mature. The wet woodland in the bed of the Holm Foot pond has become one of the richest habitats in the valley, its standing water and fallen timber supporting breeding birds, amphibians and a varied flora. The fulling mill building has been converted into dwellings, its wheel-pit kept open beneath a glass floor. At Kettlewick the bobbin mill has been restored and holds working lathes that turn wood on certain days of the summer.

The villages have changed in character rather than in form. Sallowby retains its terraces, its chapels and its market cross, though several chapels have become houses and the cooperative store is now a café. Marrow End keeps its station building as a private house beside the path, and the auction mart has been replaced by housing set around a small green. Skelmoor and Garthwaite, which had dwindled through the twentieth century, now include holiday cottages and the homes of people who travel daily to work in the towns. Pennock Bridge, too narrow for modern traffic, has been bypassed by a concrete road bridge a short distance upstream, and the old structure carries only walkers. It stands as it has for five centuries, its two phases of masonry plainly visible from the bank, the river passing beneath it toward the viaduct, the meadows and the confluence beyond Brackham.
